# audi-arg3-succession-rust

The successive-execution timing measurement (`../succession`) in Rust, on the
run model of `../rust`: one tokio task per robot, the vendored Rust client
instead of the NOVA Python SDK, the same shared operator UI. Every cycle is
one short out-and-back joint move; every step of its execution is stamped and
reported per cycle as the same `PHASES {json}` record and `SUMMARY` table the
Python twin writes, so one summarizer reads both logs side by side.

| variant | talks to NOVA via | what "execute" is |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `../succession` (audi-arg3-succession) | NOVA Python SDK | `MotionGroup.execute()` with the SDK's one-shot cursor |
| this (audi-arg3-succession-rust) | Rust client (`vendor/`) | the raw protocol: `add_trajectory` (or inline), execution websocket, completion from the state stream |

## Run it

```bash
cargo build --release           # binary embeds the static UI
NOVA_API=http://<nova-host> cargo run --release
# open http://localhost:3000/ui
```

`GET /api/health` tells you which instance and cell the app is actually
talking to. Confirm the controllers are virtual before starting anything that
moves.

Configuration (same names as `../rust`): `NOVA_API`, `NOVA_ACCESS_TOKEN`,
`CELL_NAME`, `BASE_PATH`, `PORT`, `LOG_DIR`, `LOG_MAX_BYTES`,
`LOG_BACKUP_COUNT`, `TCP` (=1), `WAIT_IO` (=start), `STOP_IO` (=stop),
`MOTION_TIMEOUT_S` (=300), `STATE_RESPONSE_RATE_MS` (=0), `LOG_LEVEL`,
`STATUS_SUBJECT`. Run-option defaults: `CYCLES` (0), `SUMMARY_EVERY` (10),
`FRAMES_MAX_BYTES` (50 MB), `DEGREES` (5), `TCP_VELOCITY_MM_S` (600),
`TCP_ACCELERATION_MM_S2` (3000), `TCP_JERK_MM_S3` (30000), `MAX_MOTION_S` (2).

## Run options

The Python twin's set, plus `transport`, which only exists here:

| option | default | what it varies |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `mode` | plan-once | where the trajectory comes from each cycle: `plan-each` (re-plan), `plan-once` (plan before the loop, reuse), `store` (plan once, write it to the store-object service, read it back before every execution) |
| `stream` | reopen | the motion-group state websocket across executions: `reopen` (opened and dropped per execution) or `persistent` (opened once before the loop and read by every execution). The Python twin's `linger` has no counterpart: the Rust client has no shared stream to keep alive |
| `transport` | cached | how the trajectory reaches the controller: `cached` calls `add_trajectory` and sends the id in `InitializeMovementRequest` (what the Python SDK does, hence the `add_trajectory` phase); `inline` sends the `JointTrajectory` in the request (what `../rust` does, no REST call) |
| `cycles` | 0 | executions per run; 0 = until the stop IO |
| `degrees` / `direction` | 5, positive | the joint-0 rotation (presets 1/2/3/5/10/15/20/45/90) |
| `velocity` / `acceleration` / `jerk` | 600 / 3000 / 30000 | the planner's TCP limits for the move (5° at these is 1.6 s on a KR270) |
| `max_motion_s` | 2 | refuse a planned move longer than this before anything moves (0 = unchecked) |
| `state_rate_ms` | 0 (step rate) | the state stream's `response_rate`; 0 omits the parameter, like every sibling |
| `gap_ms` | 0 | idle time between cycles |
| `summary_every` | 10 | log a `SUMMARY` table every N cycles (0 = only at the end) |
| `record_frames` | off | also write every state frame to `<controller>-frames.log` (capped) |

The start IO is waited on **once** before the loop and the stop IO is polled
between cycles. A cell where the start IO cannot be read runs ungated with a
warning and without the stop poll -- the Python twin does the same, so the two
stay comparable; `../rust` fails loudly instead, because there the gate is a
safety feature of the production cell.

## Reading a log

Same lines as `../succession`: configuration and client version first, then
per cycle

```
ir340r01: cycle 12 -- execute() 1812 ms | add_trajectory=49 ws_open=69 init=31 start_latency=35 motion=1590 end_detect=1 teardown=38 | frames=405 own=404 socket_opens=1
ir340r01: PHASES {"cycle": 12, "motion_id": "...", "phases": {...}, ...}
```

and every `summary_every` cycles (and at the end) a `SUMMARY` block plus a
`SUMMARY_JSON` line. `ANOMALY` on a cycle line means a stale END frame of this
trajectory before any RUNNING frame, an error, a wrong final location, or a
robot that never moved.

Phase definitions are in `src/timing.rs` (the Python twin's table applies, with
one difference: `ws_open` here is the execution websocket connect only, from the
add_trajectory answer -- or the call, with `transport=inline` -- to the
`InitializeMovementRequest`; the SDK's cursor setup that the Python phase also
covers has no counterpart). `stream_close` stamps the moment the per-execution
state socket is dropped; the client has no close handshake for it.

With `transport=inline` the trajectory id is not known before the first frame:
own frames are those carrying an id different from the previous execution's.

## Offline analysis

The Python twin's summarizer reads these logs as well:

```bash
cd ../succession && uv run python scripts/summarize_log.py <controller>.log [more logs...]
```

## Deploy

Exactly like `../rust`: `skaffold dev --cleanup=false --status-check=false`
(cross-compiles from the build host, pushes, applies `k8s/app.yaml`), or
`nova app install`. `k8s/app.yaml` sets neither `NOVA_API` nor `NATS_BROKER`
nor `BASE_PATH`; the app-operator injects them.

## The vendored client

`vendor/nova-rust-client/` is the same copy as `../rust`'s. Refresh both with
`scripts/sync-vendor.sh [path-to-client-repo]` and keep them identical, so a
difference between the two Rust apps is never the client.
EOF
cat > succession-rust/CLAUDE.md <<'EOF'
# CLAUDE.md

Read `README.md` first, then `../rust/CLAUDE.md` -- this app is built on the
Rust move-up app's foundation (client, run model, UI, logs, NATS) and inherits
its rules: never hardcode an instance, confirm virtual vs physical before
anything with physical consequences, the UI must not put work on the robots'
path, no retries around motions, the vendored client is never edited here.

## What this is

**`audi-arg3-succession-rust`** measures where the time goes between two
successive executions, through the raw protocol instead of the Python SDK. It
is the Rust twin of `../succession`: the same move, the same run options
(plus `transport`), the same `PHASES {json}` record per cycle and `SUMMARY`
statistics, so `../succession/scripts/summarize_log.py` reads both.

## What is different from `../rust`

- **`src/motion.rs`** plans a two-segment joint PTP (joint 0 out and back,
  TCP limits from the run options) instead of the move-up pose, and
  `execute()` stamps every protocol step on a `CycleTiming`. It has two
  switches the move-up app does not: `Transport` (`cached` = `add_trajectory`
  then the id, like the SDK; `inline` = the trajectory in
  `InitializeMovementRequest`, like `../rust`) and `Frames` (`Own` = a state
  socket per execution; `Shared` = the run's one socket, `stream=persistent`).
- **`src/timing.rs`** is the port of the Python `timing.py`: phases, anomaly
  rules, running statistics. Keep the phase names and the JSON keys identical
  to the Python twin's -- one summarizer reads both.
- **`src/robot.rs`** is the loop of the Python `programs.py` on `../rust`'s
  task model. The start IO is waited on once; an unreadable one runs the loop
  ungated with a warning (the Python twin's choice, for comparability) --
  `../rust` fails loudly there, on purpose, and that rule still holds for it.
- The execution FSM (`execution_fsm.rs`) is fed only frames of this
  execution's trajectory id (plus frames without an execute block, the legacy
  completion path): the previous trajectory's re-published END must never
  conclude the new one. With `transport=inline` the id is learned from the
  first frame whose id differs from the previous execution's.
- `linger` is not offered: the Rust client has no shared state-stream pump.

## Commands

```bash
cargo build --release
cargo clippy --all-targets      # keep clean
cargo fmt
cargo test                      # timing.rs + the inherited busio/logsfs/config tests
NOVA_API=http://<host> cargo run --release   # UI on :3000/ui
scripts/sync-vendor.sh          # refresh vendor/ -- keep identical to ../rust/vendor
```

## Adding a run option

Touch `runner::RunOptions`, `web::run_options` (the UI input) and
`web::run_options_from` (its parsing), `config.rs` for an env default, and
wherever `robot.rs` consumes it -- nothing else. Every value but a checkbox
arrives from the shared UI as a string.
EOF
python3 - <<'EOF'
from pathlib import Path
p = Path("README.md"); s = p.read_text()
old = "| `succession/` | `audi-arg3-succession` | NOVA Python SDK + NOVAx (its **own** pin: `lab/pause-auto-resume-main`) | one `run_program.py` process per robot |\n"
new = old + "| `succession-rust/` | `audi-arg3-succession-rust` | Rust client (vendored, same copy as `rust/`) | one tokio task per robot |\n"
assert old in s; s = s.replace(old, new)
old = "`examples/lab/succession` as an app, so the numbers can be taken on the IPC.\n"
new = old + "\n`succession-rust/` is the same measurement through the raw protocol instead of\nthe SDK (the way `rust/` relates to `sdk/`), with the same per-cycle `PHASES`\nrecord so one summarizer compares the two.\n"
assert old in s; s = s.replace(old, new)
s = s.replace("scripts/sync-ui.sh          # copy into rust/, api/, sdk/, tcpswitch/, pause/, pause-api/, succession/ static",
              "scripts/sync-ui.sh          # copy into rust/, api/, sdk/, tcpswitch/, pause/, pause-api/, succession/, succession-rust/ static")
s = s.replace("pause-api blue, succession teal-green),", "pause-api blue, succession teal-green, succession-rust copper),")
p.write_text(s)
EOF

The Rust variant is done, verified against the virtual ir340r01, and reads into the same summarizer as the Python app.

**What exists now**: `~/1prj/audi/arg3-longterm-tests/succession-rust/`, deploying as `audi-arg3-succession-rust`. It is built on `rust/` the way `succession/` is built on `pause/`: the same vendored Rust client, NATS hub, per-robot log files, log viewer, IO create, UI serving, skaffold and k8s files, all copied and renamed. New or rewritten:

- `src/timing.rs`: the port of the Python `timing.py`. Same phase names, same `PHASES {json}` keys, same statistics, with unit tests for the stats and for learning the trajectory id from frames.
- `src/motion.rs`: plans the joint-0 out-and-back move with the run's TCP limits and executes it over the raw protocol with every step stamped. The state socket is opened concurrently with `add_trajectory` and the execution connect, as the SDK does. The execution FSM only sees frames of this execution's id, so a re-published END of the previous trajectory cannot conclude the new one.
- `src/robot.rs`: the loop of the Python `programs.py` on the one-task-per-robot model, with the 2 s motion guard, the store mode, the summary blocks and a capped frames file.
- `web.rs`, `runner.rs`, `config.rs`: the run options with validation, and env defaults.

**Run options**: the Python twin's set (mode, stream, cycles, degrees, direction, velocity, acceleration, jerk, max_motion_s, state_rate_ms, gap_ms, summary_every, record_frames) plus one that only makes sense here. `transport=cached` calls `add_trajectory` and sends the id, which is what the SDK does and what gives the `add_trajectory` phase. `transport=inline` sends the trajectory in the init request, which is what the existing Rust app does. `stream` offers reopen and persistent only; linger has no counterpart because the Rust client has no shared stream pump. That, and the `ws_open` phase covering only the execution connect, is documented in the README.

**Verified on 172.31.10.89** (virtual KR270, 5°, 1.57 s move), medians in ms:

| variant | add_trajectory | ws_open | start_latency | execute() |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| plan-once reopen cached | 40 | 60 | 35 | 1746 |
| plan-once persistent cached | 41 | 59 | 33 | 1747 |
| plan-once reopen inline | – | 62 | 34 | 1776 |
| store reopen inline | – | 65 | 33 | 1779 |
| plan-each persistent inline | – | 63 | 35 | 1780 |

End detection and teardown are 0 ms here: the first END frame arrives at standstill, the FSM concludes on it, and dropping the sockets costs nothing. A 90° run was refused before motion at 17.25 s versus the 2 s bound. `cargo clippy` is clean, 27 tests pass, and the Python `summarize_log.py` produces the same table from a Rust log.

**Housekeeping**: a new accent colour for the variant went into `ui/style.css` and was synced into every app's `static/`. The root README lists the new app. Nothing is committed.

# Successive execution timing: Python SDK vs Rust client, on the IPC

Measured 2026-10-27 on ir340r01 at the IPC (NOVA 26.8.0-92) with the two
succession apps running in-cluster (`skaffold dev`), driven through their
`/api/run` by `succession/scripts/drive_runs.py`. One move: joint 0 by 5°
and back at TCP limits 600 / 3000 / 30000, planned as a 1.572 s trajectory
of 394 samples by both apps (same planner call, same limits). 30 cycles per
run, state stream at the controller step rate, no anomaly in any run.

Logs: `succession/runs-ipc-day2/{py,rust-cached,rust-inline}/`; report with
the per-cycle timelines and distributions:
`succession/runs-ipc-day2/py-vs-rust.html`.

- `py` = `audi-arg3-succession` (wandelbots-nova 6.1.0 @ lab/pause-auto-resume-main,
  one `run_program.py` process per robot, `MotionGroup.execute()` with the
  SDK's one-shot cursor).
- `rust-cached` = `audi-arg3-succession-rust` with `transport=cached`
  (`add_trajectory`, then the id in `InitializeMovementRequest` -- the SDK's
  shape). `rust-inline` sends the trajectory inside the init request.

## Medians per phase, ms

| phase | py reopen | rust cached reopen | rust inline reopen | py persistent | rust cached persistent | py linger | py plan-each | rust plan-each | py store | rust store |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| prepare (plan / store read) | – | – | – | – | – | – | 45.0 | 40.4 | 3.6 | 2.4 |
| add_trajectory | 7.2 | 2.4 | – | 7.5 | 2.1 | 7.4 | 7.3 | 2.3 | 7.2 | 2.3 |
| ws_open (execution socket) | 2.7 | 0.5 | 0.9 | 2.1 | 0.6 | 2.1 | 2.9 | 0.6 | 2.8 | 0.5 |
| init handshake | 1.9 | 2.0 | 5.9 | 1.8 | 1.7 | 1.8 | 1.9 | 1.8 | 1.8 | 1.7 |
| start handshake | 3.6 | 6.5 | 5.4 | 3.6 | 6.9 | 3.6 | 4.1 | 6.4 | 4.1 | 4.7 |
| start → first RUNNING | 11.6 | 14.4 | 13.3 | 11.7 | 14.9 | 11.7 | 11.6 | 14.3 | 11.7 | 12.6 |
| motion | 1580.0 | 1580.0 | 1580.0 | 1580.0 | 1580.0 | 1580.0 | 1580.0 | 1580.0 | 1580.0 | 1580.0 |
| END frame → resolved | 0.4 | 0.0 | 0.0 | 0.4 | 0.0 | 0.3 | 0.4 | 0.0 | 0.4 | 0.0 |
| teardown | 2.1 | 0.1 | 0.1 | 2.1 | 0.0 | 2.1 | 2.1 | 0.1 | 2.1 | 0.1 |
| state socket open → first frame | 6.2 | 4.9 | 6.9 | – | – | 13.9 (once) | 4.1 | 4.8 | 4.1 | 5.1 |
| **execute()** | **1610.0** | **1599.3** | **1599.3** | **1606.6** | **1599.3** | **1606.4** | **1609.9** | **1599.0** | **1609.2** | **1597.2** |
| execute() max | 1619.6 | 1603.3 | 1603.4 | 1617.6 | 1603.4 | 1618.1 | 1622.1 | 1603.2 | 1619.7 | 1605.0 |
| execute() jitter (max − min) | 13.3 | 4.2 | 4.5 | 11.8 | 4.4 | 14.7 | 14.8 | 5.2 | 13.3 | 8.1 |
| cycle (call → next call) | 1612.0 | 1600.0 | 1600.1 | 1608.7 | 1600.0 | 1608.3 | 1655.8 | 1640.1 | 1614.9 | 1600.3 |

(`rust inline persistent`: execute 1599.3, jitter 4.5 -- same as cached.)

## What it says

- **Both clients add very little to a 1.580 s motion.** The SDK's execute()
  is 1610 ms, the Rust client's 1599 ms: 30 ms versus 19 ms of overhead
  per execution. The 11 ms difference is `add_trajectory` (7.2 vs 2.4 ms:
  the Python client serializes and posts 394 samples through pydantic and
  aiohttp, the Rust one through serde and reqwest), the execution websocket
  connect (2.7 vs 0.5 ms), teardown (2.1 vs 0.1 ms: the SDK unwinds a task
  group and closes its shared-stream subscription, the Rust app drops two
  sockets) and the cursor's completion decision (0.4 ms vs 0: the SDK's
  state machine runs a standstill debounce on the END frame, the Rust FSM
  concludes on it).
- **The Rust app pays a little more on the wire side**: start handshake
  6.5 vs 3.6 ms and start → first RUNNING 14.4 vs 11.6 ms. The ~3 ms is the
  same in every Rust run and absent in every Python run; the Rust client
  reads the execution socket and the state stream in one `select!` loop,
  and a StartMovementResponse that arrives behind a burst of 4 ms state
  frames is seen later. It does not delay the robot: `motion` is identical
  to the millisecond, and the execution total is still 11 ms lower.
- **Jitter**: the Rust runs vary by 4–5 ms over 30 cycles, the Python runs
  by 12–15 ms. The Python spread is in add_trajectory and the handshakes
  (GC and event-loop scheduling of a 400-sample trajectory), not in the
  motion.
- **Stream lifecycle does not matter in either client.** reopen, persistent
  and linger (Python) and reopen, persistent (Rust) agree within 1 ms on the
  median: the state socket opens in 4–7 ms in parallel with add_trajectory
  and the execution connect, in both.
- **Inline vs cached (Rust)**: sending the trajectory in the init request
  saves the 2.4 ms `add_trajectory` call but makes the init handshake 4 ms
  longer (5.9 vs 2.0 ms: the controller validates the trajectory inside the
  handshake instead of in the REST call). Net zero: 1599.3 ms both ways.
- **Re-planning costs 45 ms (Python) / 40 ms (Rust); reading the stored
  trajectory 3.6 / 2.4 ms** per cycle, on top of execute().
- **End detection is not a problem in either client**: the first END frame
  already arrives at standstill on this controller (`end_settle` 0), and
  both clients resolve within 0.4 ms of it.

## Against yesterday's numbers

Yesterday's Python runs (10°, 200 / 500 / 2500, a 6.85 s trajectory of
1710 samples) showed add_trajectory 28 ms, init 6.4 ms, teardown 4.9 ms,
~58 ms overhead. Today's 30 ms is the same code on a trajectory a quarter
the size: add_trajectory, init and teardown scale with the trajectory's
sample count. Phases that do not touch the trajectory (start latency
11.7 ms, end detection 0.4 ms) are identical on both days.

content.text:
Both matrices ran clean on ir340r01 and the comparison is written up.

**Where it lives**

- Report with per-cycle timelines and distributions: https://claude.ai/artifact/G3ZnTxyWHubYE4K5mkrY5n (private until you share it), also at `succession/runs-ipc-day2/py-vs-rust.html`.
- Write-up: `docs/succession-py-vs-rust.md` in the Audi repo.
- Logs: `succession/runs-ipc-day2/{py,rust-cached,rust-inline}/`, 30 cycles each, zero anomalies.

**Headline numbers** (medians in ms, 5° move, 1.572 s planned, same planner call in both apps):

| phase | Python SDK | Rust client (cached) |
|---|---|---|
| add_trajectory | 7.2 | 2.4 |
| execution socket open | 2.7 | 0.5 |
| init handshake | 1.9 | 2.0 |
| start → first RUNNING | 11.6 | 14.4 |
| motion | 1580.0 | 1580.0 |
| END frame → resolved | 0.4 | 0.0 |
| teardown | 2.1 | 0.1 |
| execute() | 1610.0 | 1599.3 |
| execute() jitter over 30 cycles | 13.3 | 4.2 |

**What it says**

- The SDK adds about 30 ms per execution, the Rust client about 19 ms. The 11 ms gap is add_trajectory serialization, the websocket connect, the task-group teardown and the cursor's standstill debounce. None of it is end detection: both clients resolve within half a millisecond of the first END frame, which already arrives at standstill.
- The Rust app pays 3 ms more on the start handshake and start latency, consistently. It reads the execution socket and the 4 ms state stream in one select loop, so the start acknowledgement is seen behind a burst of frames. The robot is not affected: motion is identical to the millisecond.
- Stream lifecycle makes no difference in either client. Reopen, persistent and linger agree within 1 ms.
- Inline versus cached in Rust is net zero: no REST call, but the init handshake grows by the same 4 ms because the controller validates the trajectory inside it.
- Re-planning costs 45 ms (Python) or 40 ms (Rust) per cycle; a store read 3.6 or 2.4 ms.
- Compared with yesterday's 6.85 s, 1710-sample move, the SDK's add_trajectory, init and teardown dropped from 28, 6.4 and 4.9 ms to 7.2, 1.9 and 2.1 ms. Those phases scale with trajectory size; start latency and end detection did not change.

**Two things on the way**: the Rust runs initially aborted in the driver because its status has no `exit_code` field, fixed in `drive_runs.py` and re-run. The gate IO `start` is back at false on the cell. Nothing is committed in the repo.
